title: Hip, Gluteal Region & Thigh
summary: Learn how the hip and thigh support body weight and power walking, running and standing.

lessons.title: Pelvic Girdle, Proximal Femur & the Hip Joint

levels.kid:
Your hips are where your legs join your body. The big bowl-shaped bones there are called the **pelvis**. Each side has a deep cup in it.

The top of your thigh bone, the **femur**, has a round ball on the end. The ball fits snugly into the cup, like a ball sitting in a deep bowl. This is called a **ball-and-socket joint**.

Because the cup is deep, the ball stays put even when you jump. Strong straps called **ligaments** wrap around it like tight ropes. That makes your hip very steady.

The ball can still swing forward, backward, out to the side and twist. That's how you can walk, kick a ball and sit down.
levels.hs:
The **pelvic girdle** connects the legs to the trunk. It is made of two **hip bones** (coxal bones) that join the **sacrum** at the back and each other at the front, at the **pubic symphysis**. Each hip bone forms from three bones that fuse in the teen years: the **ilium** (the wide upper wing), the **ischium** (the part you sit on) and the **pubis** (the front part).

All three meet at the **acetabulum**, a deep cup-shaped socket. The **head of the femur** fits into it, forming the **hip joint**, a **synovial ball-and-socket joint**.

Key parts of the proximal femur:
- **Head**: the smooth ball
- **Neck**: the narrow bridge angled toward the pelvis
- **Greater and lesser trochanters**: bumps where muscles attach

The hip trades some movement for stability, the opposite of the shoulder. Its socket is deep, a rim of cartilage called the **labrum** deepens it further, and three strong ligaments reinforce the capsule. The hip can flex, extend, abduct, adduct and rotate.

Real example: in older adults with weak bones (osteoporosis), a fall onto the side often breaks the **femoral neck**. This is called a "hip fracture." It is serious because the bone's blood supply may be damaged.
levels.college:
**Pelvic girdle.** Each **os coxae** forms from ilium, ischium and pubis, which meet at a **Y-shaped triradiate cartilage** in the acetabulum. This cartilage fuses around ages 15-17. Important landmarks include:
- **ASIS** (anterior superior iliac spine) and the iliac crest
- **Ischial tuberosity** and ischial spine
- **Greater and lesser sciatic notches**, which the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments convert into foramina
- **Obturator foramen**, mostly closed by a membrane

**Proximal femur.** The **head** bears the **fovea**, the attachment for the **ligament of the head (ligamentum teres)**. The **neck-shaft angle** is about 125-130 degrees in adults. **Femoral anteversion** (the neck angled forward) is about 10-15 degrees. The greater and lesser trochanters are linked by the **intertrochanteric line** at the front and the **intertrochanteric crest** at the back.

**The joint.**
- The **acetabulum** is lunate (horseshoe-shaped) articular cartilage around a non-articular **acetabular fossa**, which holds a fat pad.
- The **acetabular labrum** and the **transverse acetabular ligament** complete the rim.
- The capsule attaches to the intertrochanteric line at the front. At the back it attaches only partway down the neck.
- **Iliofemoral ligament (Y ligament of Bigelow)**: the strongest ligament in the body. It limits hyperextension, letting you stand with little muscle effort.
- **Pubofemoral ligament** limits abduction. **Ischiofemoral ligament** limits internal rotation.
- All three spiral, tightening in extension. This makes extension with internal rotation the **close-packed position**.

**Blood supply.** Most arterial blood reaches the head through **retinacular arteries**, chiefly from the **medial circumflex femoral artery**. These vessels run up the neck under the capsule. The artery of the ligamentum teres, from the obturator artery, contributes little in adults.
levels.phd:
**Biomechanics.** In single-leg stance, the hip carries roughly 2.5-3 times body weight. During running, joint loads exceed 4-5 times body weight. These figures were confirmed by Bergmann's instrumented prosthesis studies. The load is high because the abductor lever arm is shorter than the body-weight lever arm. The neck-shaft angle and **femoral offset** set this abductor moment arm. **Coxa vara** (a smaller angle) lengthens the lever arm but raises bending stress on the neck. **Coxa valga** shortens the lever arm. This is why a cane held in the opposite hand reduces joint load so effectively.

**Trabecular architecture.** The proximal femur shows **Wolff's law** in action. Several trabecular systems line up along the paths of stress:
- **Principal compressive group**: runs from the medial cortex into the superior head
- **Principal tensile group**: arcs from the lateral cortex
- **Ward's triangle**: a relatively sparse zone between them, which thins early in osteoporosis
- **Calcar femorale**: a dense vertical plate of bone that reinforces the posteromedial neck

**Vascular anatomy.** The deep branch of the **medial circumflex femoral artery** passes posterior to obturator externus and anterior to the short external rotators. It then pierces the capsule and gives off the posterosuperior retinacular vessels. Gautier and Ganz (2000) defined this course precisely, which enabled **surgical hip dislocation** without causing osteonecrosis. Displaced **intracapsular neck fractures** tear these vessels, so they carry a high risk of nonunion and **avascular necrosis**. Extracapsular intertrochanteric fractures do not.

**Labrum and seal.** The fibrocartilaginous labrum creates a negative-pressure **suction seal** and limits synovial fluid outflow. This helps keep fluid pressurized within the joint. Its articular side is poorly vascularized, which limits healing.

**Development.** The acetabulum and femoral head shape each other during growth. Formation of the acetabulum depends on the head sitting concentrically in the socket. If they do not stay aligned, the result is **developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)**: a shallow socket with reduced coverage of the head.
levels.expert:
**Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI).** Ganz and colleagues (2003) proposed that subtle abnormal shapes cause early osteoarthritis. There are two main types:
- **Cam**: an aspherical bump at the head-neck junction. It is linked to vigorous adolescent sport while the growth plate is still open.
- **Pincer**: acetabular overcoverage, such as retroversion or a crossover sign on X-ray.

In cam impingement, the bump shears the cartilage at the edge of the socket, peeling it from the labrum. Imaging uses the **alpha angle** (abnormal above about 55-60 degrees) and the **lateral center-edge angle of Wiberg**. A value below about 20 degrees suggests dysplasia, while one above about 40 degrees suggests overcoverage. A key open question: cam shape is common in people with no symptoms. Trials such as UK FASHIoN found that arthroscopy beat physiotherapy only modestly, so patient selection remains debated.

**Dysplasia surgery.** The **Bernese periacetabular osteotomy** reorients the acetabulum while preserving the posterior column. Results are best before significant osteoarthritis develops.

**Fracture pitfalls.**
- Occult neck fractures in osteoporotic bone are often missed on X-ray. MRI is the preferred next test.
- Garden and Pauwels classifications guide treatment: fixation versus arthroplasty.
- **Atypical subtrochanteric fractures** are associated with long-term bisphosphonate use.
- **Slipped capital femoral epiphysis** in adolescents can present only as knee pain. The pain is referred through the obturator and femoral nerves, illustrating **Hilton's law**.

**Surgical approaches.** The posterior approach endangers the sciatic nerve and the posterior capsule, which raises dislocation risk unless the capsule is repaired. The direct anterior approach risks the **lateral femoral cutaneous nerve**.

**Avascular necrosis** can also occur without fracture. Causes include corticosteroids, alcohol-related disease and sickle cell disease. Diagnosis relies on MRI, staged by the Ficat or ARCO systems.

Frontiers include hip-preservation imaging and research on cartilage biomarkers.

keyPoints: Each hip bone forms from ilium, ischium and pubis meeting at the acetabulum
The hip is a deep synovial ball-and-socket joint built for stability
Labrum and transverse acetabular ligament deepen and complete the socket
Iliofemoral ligament is the strongest in the body and limits hyperextension
The femoral head is supplied mainly by the medial circumflex femoral artery via retinacular vessels
Displaced femoral neck fractures risk avascular necrosis

test.q: Which three bones fuse to form each hip bone?
test.explain: The os coxae forms from the ilium, ischium and pubis, which meet at the acetabulum. The sacrum and coccyx belong to the vertebral column.

test.q: What type of joint is the hip?
test.explain: The femoral head (ball) fits into the acetabulum (socket) in a synovial joint.

test.q: Which ligament limits hip hyperextension and is the strongest in the body?
test.explain: The Y-shaped iliofemoral ligament of Bigelow resists hyperextension. The pubofemoral ligament limits abduction instead.

test.q: Which artery supplies most of the adult femoral head?
test.explain: Retinacular branches, mainly from the medial circumflex femoral artery, supply the head. The obturator artery's branch in the ligamentum teres contributes little in adults.

test.q: What is the role of the acetabular labrum?
choices: It forms the femoral head surface
It deepens and seals the socket
It joins the hip bone to sacrum
test.explain: The fibrocartilage labrum deepens the acetabulum and creates a suction seal.

test.q: The normal adult femoral neck-shaft angle is about:
test.explain: Adults average about 125-130 degrees. A smaller angle is coxa vara and a larger one is coxa valga.

test.q: Why do displaced femoral neck fractures risk avascular necrosis?
choices: They compress the femoral vein in the thigh
They damage the sciatic nerve behind the hip
They tear retinacular vessels along the neck
They block the obturator foramen membrane
test.explain: The retinacular arteries run up the neck under the capsule, so intracapsular displacement disrupts the head's blood supply.

test.q: Compared with the shoulder, the hip mainly favors:
test.explain: A deep socket and strong ligaments make the hip stable at some cost to range of movement.

test.q: Where do the ilium, ischium and pubis meet?
test.explain: They meet at a triradiate cartilage in the acetabulum, which fuses in the teen years.

test.q: The large bump on the lateral proximal femur where muscles attach is the greater ___.
test.explain: The greater and lesser trochanters are muscle attachment sites.

test.q: What is the name of the cup-shaped socket of the hip bone?
test.explain: The acetabulum receives the femoral head.

test.q: The joint where the two hip bones meet at the front is the pubic ___.
test.explain: The pubic symphysis is a cartilaginous joint joining the two pubic bones.

kidTest.q: What kind of joint is your hip?
kidTest.explain: The round top of the femur sits in a cup in the pelvis.

kidTest.q: What is the big thigh bone called?
kidTest.explain: The femur is your thigh bone.

kidTest.q: What holds the hip joint tightly together?
kidTest.explain: Ligaments act like tight ropes around the joint.

kidTest.q: Why does the ball stay put when you jump?
kidTest.explain: A deep cup holds the ball steady.

kidTest.q: The big bowl-shaped bones at your hips are the p _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The pelvis connects your legs to your body.

advancedTest.q: Why is an intertrochanteric fracture less likely to cause osteonecrosis than a displaced subcapital fracture?
choices: It is protected by the iliofemoral ligament from any displacement
It spares the labrum, which supplies most of the head's blood
It lies outside the retinacular supply route to the head
It heals faster because the obturator artery feeds the trochanters
advancedTest.explain: Intertrochanteric fractures are extracapsular, distal to where the retinacular vessels ascend the neck. Subcapital fractures tear those vessels.

advancedTest.q: Holding a cane in the hand opposite a painful hip reduces joint load mainly because it:
choices: Shifts load from the labrum onto the acetabular fossa
Increases femoral anteversion during the stance phase
Reduces the abductor force needed to balance the pelvis
Tightens the iliofemoral ligament to carry body weight
advancedTest.explain: The joint load is dominated by abductor force acting on a short lever arm. A contralateral cane supplies a counter-moment, reducing the abductor force required.

advancedTest.q: Gautier and Ganz's mapping of the medial circumflex femoral artery mattered surgically because it:
choices: Demonstrated that cam lesions arise from obturator ischemia
Proved the labrum's articular side is richly vascularized
Showed the ligamentum teres artery is the dominant adult supply
Enabled safe surgical hip dislocation that preserves head perfusion
advancedTest.explain: Knowing the deep branch's course relative to obturator externus and the short rotators let surgeons dislocate the hip without causing avascular necrosis.

advancedTest.q: Why is selecting patients for arthroscopic FAI surgery controversial?
choices: Cam morphology is often present in people without symptoms
Trials showed arthroscopy is inferior to physiotherapy
Pincer lesions show up on imaging after hip replacement
The alpha angle measures acetabular depth rather than shape
advancedTest.explain: Cam shape is common in asymptomatic people, and trials like UK FASHIoN found only modest benefit over physiotherapy, not inferiority.

lessons.title: Gluteal Muscles & Deep Lateral Rotators

levels.kid:
Your bottom is made of some of the strongest muscles in your body! They are called the **gluteal muscles**, or glutes for short.

The biggest one, **gluteus maximus**, is like a powerful engine. It helps you climb stairs, jump, and stand up from a chair.

Two smaller glutes sit on the side of your hip. They work like a helper holding a see-saw level. When you stand on one foot, they stop your hips from tipping over.

Deep underneath are small muscles that twist your leg so your toes point outward. One of them, the **piriformis**, sits right beside a big nerve that runs down your leg. That nerve is called the **sciatic nerve**.

That is why doctors give shots in the upper outer part of the bottom, safely away from the nerve.
levels.hs:
The **gluteal region** (buttock) sits behind the pelvis and moves the hip joint. Its muscles fall into three layers.

- **Gluteus maximus**: the largest, most superficial muscle. It **extends** the hip (swings the thigh backward) and laterally rotates it. It works hardest when you climb stairs, run, or rise from sitting, and much less during easy walking on flat ground. It is supplied by the **inferior gluteal nerve**.
- **Gluteus medius and minimus**: on the side of the hip. They **abduct** the thigh (move it away from the midline). More importantly, they keep the pelvis level when you stand on one leg. They share the **superior gluteal nerve**, along with a small muscle called tensor fasciae latae.
- **Deep lateral rotators**: six small muscles that turn the thigh outward. From top to bottom they are piriformis, superior gemellus, obturator internus, inferior gemellus, quadratus femoris and (deepest) obturator externus.

Real example: if the superior gluteal nerve is damaged, the hip drops on the opposite side whenever the patient stands on the injured side. This is a positive **Trendelenburg sign**.

The **piriformis** is the key landmark. Most nerves and vessels leaving the pelvis pass above or below it. That includes the **sciatic nerve**, which normally exits below piriformis.
levels.college:
**Openings.** Gluteal structures leave the pelvis through the **greater sciatic foramen**. The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments turn the sciatic notches into this foramen and the **lesser sciatic foramen**. Piriformis fills the greater foramen and divides it:
- **Suprapiriform**: superior gluteal nerve and vessels.
- **Infrapiriform**: inferior gluteal nerve and vessels, sciatic nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels, and the nerves to obturator internus and quadratus femoris.

The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels hook around the sacrospinous ligament. They then re-enter through the lesser foramen to reach the perineum. The obturator internus tendon exits through that same lesser foramen.

**Muscles.**
- **Gluteus maximus** arises from the ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, the sacrum, the coccyx and the sacrotuberous ligament. Most of it inserts into the **iliotibial tract**, with deeper fibres attaching to the gluteal tuberosity. Actions: hip extension and lateral rotation. Through the iliotibial tract it also helps steady the extended knee. Nerve: inferior gluteal (L5-S2).
- **Gluteus medius and minimus** run from the outer ilium to the greater trochanter. They abduct the hip and, through their anterior fibres, medially rotate it. Nerve: superior gluteal (L4-S1). The same nerve supplies **tensor fasciae latae**.
- **Lateral rotators.** Piriformis is supplied by S1-S2. Obturator internus and superior gemellus share one nerve; quadratus femoris and inferior gemellus share another. Obturator externus is supplied by the **obturator nerve**.

**Function in gait.** During single-leg stance, the abductors on the stance side pull down on the ilium to keep the opposite hip from sagging. Abductor weakness causes a **Trendelenburg gait**. Patients may also lurch their trunk over the weak side to shorten the lever arm.

**Injections.** Intramuscular injections go into the **superolateral quadrant** or the ventrogluteal site (gluteus medius). Both lie away from the sciatic nerve.
levels.phd:
**Abductor biomechanics.** In single-leg stance, the abductors balance a moment arm from body weight that is roughly 2-3 times longer than their own. As a result, the joint reaction force reaches about 2.5-3 times body weight. This is Pauwels' classic analysis, later confirmed by Bergmann's instrumented hip prostheses. It explains why a cane held in the **contralateral** hand helps so much: the cane creates a counter-moment that lowers both abductor demand and joint load.

**Rotator function depends on hip position.** Piriformis is a lateral rotator in extension. Beyond about 60-90 degrees of flexion, its line of action passes the axis and it becomes a medial rotator and abductor. The deep rotators are short, with large cross-sectional areas, and lie close to the joint. These features suggest they act mainly as dynamic stabilisers that compress the femoral head into the acetabulum, a role often compared to the rotator cuff.

**Sciatic-piriformis variants.** In classic cadaver series and later meta-analyses, the sciatic nerve passes below piriformis in roughly 85-90% of limbs. In most variants the **common fibular division** pierces piriformis or passes above it, while the tibial division passes below. This anatomy underlies the proposed **piriformis syndrome**, a type of **deep gluteal syndrome**. The term is controversial because there are no validated diagnostic criteria, and many patients have fibrous bands or other compressors rather than piriformis itself.

**Gluteus maximus and human evolution.** The human gluteus maximus is greatly enlarged compared with that of chimpanzees. EMG studies (Lieberman and colleagues, 2006) show it is fairly quiet in level walking but strongly recruited in running. There it controls trunk pitch and decelerates the swing limb. This supports the endurance-running hypothesis, which argues that the muscle expanded for running rather than for walking upright.

**Vascular anastomoses.** The superior and inferior gluteal arteries come from the internal iliac artery. They join with the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries and the first perforating artery to form the **cruciate** and **trochanteric anastomoses**. These connections provide collateral flow around the hip.
levels.expert:
**Greater trochanteric pain syndrome.** Lateral hip pain once labelled "trochanteric bursitis" usually reflects **gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy** or tears. Some call these "rotator cuff tears of the hip." The tears tend to be degenerative, are common in middle-aged women, and favour the anterior fibres of medius and the minimus footprint. The best clinical clues are pain within 30 seconds of single-leg stance and resisted external derotation. MRI shows tendon changes, but these correlate imperfectly with symptoms. Endoscopic and open repairs, sometimes augmented, give good results in selected patients. Repeated corticosteroid injections risk weakening the tendon.

**Surgical approaches to the hip.**
- **Posterior (Kocher-Langenbeck/Moore)**: the surgeon splits gluteus maximus and releases the short external rotators. Repairing the capsule and rotators lowers dislocation rates after arthroplasty. The sciatic nerve is at risk and is protected by retracting the reflected rotators over it.
- **Direct lateral (Hardinge)**: elevates the anterior part of gluteus medius. The superior gluteal nerve runs about 3-5 cm above the greater trochanter, so splitting medius higher than this risks denervating tensor fasciae latae and anterior medius, producing a limp.
- **Direct anterior**: uses the internervous plane between tensor fasciae latae (superior gluteal nerve) and sartorius (femoral nerve). It spares the abductors, but the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is at risk.
- **Ganz trochanteric flip osteotomy**: enables surgical dislocation of the hip. The obturator externus is preserved because the **deep branch of the medial circumflex femoral artery** crosses behind it. That branch is the main supply to the femoral head.

**Iatrogenic sciatic injury.** Intramuscular injections given in the inferomedial quadrant can injure the sciatic nerve. The common fibular division is especially vulnerable, which explains why foot drop dominates these injuries. Ventrogluteal injection avoids the gluteal neurovascular bundles more reliably than dorsogluteal injection.

**Open questions.** Deep gluteal syndrome is increasingly managed by endoscopic sciatic neurolysis, but evidence comes from case series. MR neurography and diagnostic blocks still lack agreed reference standards. Dynamic imaging of nerve gliding during hip flexion and rotation is an active research area.

keyPoints: Gluteus maximus extends and laterally rotates the hip (inferior gluteal nerve)
Gluteus medius and minimus abduct the hip and level the pelvis (superior gluteal nerve)
Abductor weakness causes a positive Trendelenburg sign on the opposite side
Six deep lateral rotators: piriformis, gemelli, obturator internus, quadratus femoris, obturator externus
Piriformis divides the greater sciatic foramen; the sciatic nerve usually exits below it
Safe gluteal injections go superolaterally, away from the sciatic nerve

test.q: The main action of gluteus maximus is:
test.explain: Gluteus maximus extends the hip, as in climbing stairs, and also laterally rotates it. Hip flexion is mainly done by iliopsoas.

test.q: Which nerve supplies gluteus medius and gluteus minimus?
test.explain: The superior gluteal nerve supplies medius, minimus and tensor fasciae latae. The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus.

test.q: A patient stands on the right leg and the left hip drops. Which muscles are weak?
test.explain: The stance-side abductors keep the opposite hip level, so a left-side drop means the right abductors are weak. This is a positive Trendelenburg sign.

test.q: Which muscle is the key landmark dividing the greater sciatic foramen?
test.explain: Piriformis fills the greater sciatic foramen, creating suprapiriform and infrapiriform spaces.

test.q: Which structure passes above piriformis?
test.explain: Only the superior gluteal nerve and vessels pass above piriformis. The other nerves listed exit below it.

test.q: Most of gluteus maximus inserts into the:
test.explain: Most fibres insert into the iliotibial tract. The deeper fibres attach to the gluteal tuberosity.

test.q: Which deep lateral rotator is supplied by the obturator nerve?
test.explain: Obturator externus is supplied by the obturator nerve. Despite its similar name, obturator internus has its own nerve from the sacral plexus.

test.q: Gluteal intramuscular injections are given in the superolateral quadrant to avoid the:
test.explain: The sciatic nerve runs through the lower, inner part of the buttock, so the upper outer area is safer.

test.q: During which activity is gluteus maximus least active?
test.explain: Gluteus maximus is fairly quiet in easy level walking and strongly recruited in running, climbing and rising from sitting.

test.q: Name the sign in which the pelvis drops on the unsupported side during single-leg stance.
test.explain: A positive Trendelenburg sign indicates weak hip abductors or superior gluteal nerve injury on the stance side.

test.q: The obturator internus tendon leaves the pelvis through the ___ sciatic foramen.
test.explain: The obturator internus tendon turns around the lesser sciatic notch and exits through the lesser sciatic foramen.

test.q: Gluteus maximus is supplied by the ___ gluteal nerve.
test.explain: The inferior gluteal nerve (L5-S2) exits below piriformis to supply gluteus maximus.

kidTest.q: Where are the gluteal muscles?
kidTest.explain: The glutes are the muscles of your bottom.

kidTest.q: What does gluteus maximus help you do?
kidTest.explain: It powers climbing, jumping and standing up.

kidTest.q: What do the side glutes do when you stand on one foot?
choices: Lift your knee toward your chest
Point your toes down toward the floor
kidTest.explain: They stop your hips from tipping, like holding a see-saw level.

kidTest.q: Why are shots given in the upper outer bottom?
choices: Because the skin is thicker there
To stay away from a big nerve
Because it is the warmest place
kidTest.explain: This keeps the needle away from the sciatic nerve.

kidTest.q: The small muscle beside the big leg nerve is the p _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The piriformis sits right next to the sciatic nerve.

advancedTest.q: Why does a cane in the hand opposite a painful hip reduce joint load?
choices: It shifts body weight directly onto the painful leg
It creates a counter-moment that lowers abductor force demand
It relaxes the hip flexors that compress the joint
It lengthens the abductor moment arm by tilting the femur
advancedTest.explain: Joint reaction force mostly comes from abductor contraction. A contralateral cane supplies an opposing moment, so the abductors need to pull less hard.

advancedTest.q: A Hardinge approach splits gluteus medius 7 cm above the greater trochanter. The likely result is:
choices: Numbness of the lateral thigh skin
Foot drop from a common fibular nerve injury
Weak hip extension from inferior gluteal nerve injury
An abductor limp from superior gluteal nerve injury
advancedTest.explain: The superior gluteal nerve runs about 3-5 cm above the trochanter. A split higher than this can denervate the anterior medius and tensor fasciae latae.

advancedTest.q: Why is obturator externus preserved during a Ganz surgical hip dislocation?
choices: It shields the main artery to the femoral head
It anchors the iliotibial tract to the femur
It contains the main nerve supply to gluteus medius
The sciatic nerve runs inside its tendon sheath
advancedTest.explain: The deep branch of the medial circumflex femoral artery, the main supply to the femoral head, crosses behind obturator externus.

advancedTest.q: With the hip flexed beyond about 90 degrees, piriformis contraction mainly:
choices: Medially rotates and abducts the thigh
Laterally rotates and adducts the thigh
advancedTest.explain: In deep flexion, piriformis's line of action crosses the rotation axis, so it switches from a lateral rotator to a medial rotator and abductor.

lessons.title: Anterior Thigh, Femoral Triangle & Adductor Canal

levels.kid:
Put your hand on the front of your thigh and kick your leg out straight. Feel that big muscle getting hard? That is your **quadriceps**. "Quad" means four, because it is really four muscles working as a team. They straighten your knee so you can stand, jump and kick a ball.

Near the top of your thigh, close to where your leg joins your body, there is a special triangle-shaped space. Important tubes run through it, like pipes under a street. One pipe brings blood down to your leg. One brings blood back up. A nerve, like an electric wire, tells the quads to move.

Lower down, these pipes slip into a hidden tunnel between muscles, which keeps them safe on their way to the knee.
levels.hs:
The front of the thigh is the **anterior compartment**. Its muscles mainly **extend the knee** (straighten it), and most are controlled by the **femoral nerve**.

The key muscles:
- **Quadriceps femoris**: four heads (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius) that join into the quadriceps tendon. This tendon wraps the **patella** (kneecap) and continues as the patellar ligament to the tibia.
- **Sartorius**: the longest muscle in the body. It runs diagonally from the hip bone to the inside of the knee and helps you sit cross-legged.
- **Iliopsoas**: a strong hip flexor that lifts the thigh forward.

The **femoral triangle** is a hollow in the upper inner thigh. Its borders are the **inguinal ligament** above, the sartorius on the outer side, and the adductor longus on the inner side. From lateral to medial it holds the femoral **N**erve, **A**rtery, **V**ein and an **E**mpty space with **L**ymph nodes. Students remember this as **NAVEL**.

Real example: doctors feel the femoral pulse just below the middle of the inguinal ligament. They also thread catheters up the femoral artery to reach the heart for angiograms.

Below the triangle, the artery and vein pass into the **adductor canal**, a muscular tunnel that carries them toward the back of the knee.
levels.college:
**Anterior compartment.** It is innervated by the **femoral nerve** (L2-L4, posterior divisions of the lumbar plexus). The exception is psoas major, supplied directly by anterior rami L1-L3.
- **Rectus femoris** arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine and the area above the acetabulum. It crosses both the hip and the knee, so it flexes the hip and extends the knee.
- **Vasti** (lateralis, medialis, intermedius) arise from the femoral shaft and act only on the knee. The lowest fibres of vastus medialis are called **vastus medialis obliquus (VMO)**. They resist lateral pull on the patella.
- **Sartorius** runs from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pes anserinus. It flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip, and flexes the knee.
- **Iliopsoas** inserts on the lesser trochanter and is the main hip flexor.

**Femoral triangle.** Borders: inguinal ligament (base), medial border of sartorius (lateral), and medial border of adductor longus (medial). The floor is iliopsoas laterally and pectineus medially. The roof is fascia lata with the **saphenous opening**, where the great saphenous vein joins the femoral vein. The **femoral sheath** encloses the artery, the vein and the **femoral canal**, but not the nerve. The femoral canal contains lymph nodes (the node of Cloquet) and is the site of **femoral hernia**. The **profunda femoris** branches from the femoral artery about 3-4 cm below the ligament.

**Adductor canal (Hunter's canal).** It runs from the triangle's apex to the **adductor hiatus** in adductor magnus. Its walls are vastus medialis (anterolateral), adductor longus and magnus (posterior), and sartorius (roof). Contents: femoral artery and vein, **saphenous nerve**, and the nerve to vastus medialis. At the hiatus the vessels become the popliteal vessels. The saphenous nerve does not pass through the hiatus.
levels.phd:
**Development and fascial logic.** The femoral nerve forms from posterior divisions of the L2-L4 ventral rami. That is why it supplies the dorsal (extensor) muscle mass, which becomes anterior after the lower limb rotates medially during development. The femoral sheath is a downward extension of transversalis fascia in front of the vessels and iliac fascia behind them. Its three compartments are the arterial, venous and femoral canal. Because the nerve lies outside the sheath, behind the iliac fascia, fluid injected beneath the fascia iliaca spreads differently from fluid injected inside the sheath.

**Femoral ring.** The ring is the opening at the top of the femoral canal. Its boundaries are the lacunar ligament (medial), the femoral vein (lateral), the inguinal ligament (anterior) and the pectineal ligament (posterior). The sharp lacunar edge explains why femoral hernias strangulate more often than indirect inguinal hernias. An **aberrant obturator artery** arising from the inferior epigastric artery (the "corona mortis") may course near the ring. It is relevant when a constricting ring is incised.

**Profunda femoris variability.** The medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries usually arise from the profunda. In a substantial minority, one arises from the femoral artery itself. The lateral circumflex femoral artery's descending branch supplies the anterolateral thigh. It is the pedicle of the ALT flap, whose perforators run either through vastus lateralis (musculocutaneous) or between muscles (septocutaneous).

**Quadriceps biomechanics.** The **Q-angle** is formed by the line from the ASIS to the patellar centre and the line from the patella to the tibial tuberosity. It produces a net lateral force on the patella. Debate continues over whether VMO can be selectively strengthened. EMG studies largely fail to show isolated VMO recruitment, and this has shifted the emphasis toward hip and global quadriceps strengthening. Rectus femoris is biarticular, so its knee-extension force falls when the hip is flexed (active insufficiency).

**Adductor canal compartmentalization.** The vastoadductor membrane forms the canal's distal anterior wall. Cadaveric dye studies show variable spread from the canal to the popliteal fossa via the hiatus. This partly explains inconsistent posterior knee analgesia after block.
levels.expert:
**Femoral access.** Arterial puncture should be over the **femoral head** on fluoroscopy, below the inguinal ligament and above the bifurcation. Skin landmarks can mislead, because the skin crease and the ligament differ substantially in obese patients. A puncture that is too high risks retroperitoneal haemorrhage, which is hard to compress. One that is too low risks pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula. Ultrasound guidance reduces these complications and is now standard in many cath labs, although transradial access has displaced femoral access for many coronary procedures.

**Regional anaesthesia.** The **adductor canal block** has largely replaced the femoral nerve block for knee arthroplasty. It targets the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis but spares most quadriceps motor fibres. This preserves strength and lowers fall risk. Nomenclature is contentious. Many "adductor canal" injections at mid-thigh actually sit in the distal femoral triangle, and recent consensus work urges accurate naming. The fascia iliaca and PENG blocks are used for hip fractures.

**Nerve injury.** The femoral nerve can be compressed in its iliopsoas groove, for example by a **retroperitoneal haematoma** in anticoagulated patients, or by self-retaining retractors in pelvic surgery. Signs are quadriceps weakness, a reduced patellar reflex and anteromedial sensory loss. Hip flexion is relatively spared if the lesion lies below the iliacus branches. The **saphenous nerve** is vulnerable during great saphenous vein harvest, medial knee arthroscopy portals and adductor canal procedures, causing medial leg numbness. Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression near the ASIS) is the key differential for anterolateral thigh sensory symptoms.

**Vascular disease.** The distal superficial femoral artery at the adductor hiatus is a classic site of atherosclerotic occlusion. Proposed contributors include mechanical torsion and compression during knee flexion. Rarer **adductor canal syndrome** causes claudication in young athletes from fibrous bands. Endovascular stents here have historically fractured, which drove the development of drug-coated balloons. Their safety debate (a 2018 meta-analysis signal of mortality) has since been largely allayed by later data.

For neurosurgeons, the femoral stretch test and L3-L4 radiculopathy mimic femoral neuropathy. Paraspinal EMG distinguishes the two.

keyPoints: Anterior thigh muscles extend the knee and are supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L4)
Quadriceps = rectus femoris + three vasti; rectus femoris also flexes the hip
Femoral triangle: inguinal ligament, sartorius, adductor longus
Contents lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, canal with lymph nodes (NAVEL)
The femoral sheath holds artery, vein and femoral canal, but not the nerve
Adductor canal carries femoral vessels and saphenous nerve to the adductor hiatus

Obturator nerve entrapment in its canal
Saphenous nerve injury in the adductor canal
L4 root compression in the lateral recess

It mostly spares quadriceps motor fibres, preserving strength
It blocks the sciatic nerve and anaesthetizes the posterior knee
It acts on the obturator nerve, preventing adductor spasm

It lies over the femoral head, leaving no firm surface for pressure

The vasti switch to flexing the hip during that motion
The patellar ligament loosens and slips off the tibia
The femoral nerve becomes stretched when the hip is flexed

lessons.title: Medial Thigh: Adductors & the Obturator Nerve

levels.kid:
Squeeze your knees together like you are holding a ball between them. The muscles doing that squeeze live on the inside of your thighs. They are called **adductors**, which means "bring toward the middle."

These muscles help you stay steady when you walk, so you don't wobble side to side. Soccer players and horse riders use them a lot.

The muscles need a message wire to tell them when to squeeze. That wire is a nerve called the **obturator nerve**. It comes out of your spine and slips through a little hole in your hip bone, like a cable going through a hole in a wall.

If a player stretches too far, these muscles can get a painful pull called a **groin strain**.
levels.hs:
The **medial compartment** of the thigh is the group of muscles on the inner side of the thigh. Their main job is **adduction**: pulling the thigh toward the midline of the body.

The muscles in this group:
- **Adductor longus**: the most front-facing adductor, easy to feel as a cord in the groin
- **Adductor brevis**: short, lying just behind longus
- **Adductor magnus**: the largest, with an adductor part and a hamstring part
- **Gracilis**: a long, thin strap that crosses the knee
- **Obturator externus**: a small deep muscle that mainly rotates the thigh outward

Most of these muscles start on the pubic bone and the ischium (the lower parts of the hip bone). They attach along the back of the femur on a ridge called the **linea aspera**.

The main nerve is the **obturator nerve**. It forms from spinal nerves **L2, L3 and L4**. It leaves the pelvis through the **obturator canal**, a gap at the top of the large obturator foramen in the hip bone. It also supplies a patch of skin on the inner thigh.

Real example: a **groin pull** in soccer or ice hockey is usually a strain of adductor longus. It often happens when a player kicks hard or changes direction suddenly.
levels.college:
**Attachments.** Most adductors arise from the pubis and ischiopubic ramus and insert on the posterior femur along the **linea aspera**.
- **Pectineus**: arises from the pectineal line of the pubis. It is often grouped with the medial muscles, but it is usually innervated by the **femoral nerve**, sometimes with an obturator contribution.
- **Adductor longus**: arises from the body of the pubis and inserts on the middle third of the linea aspera. It forms the medial border of the femoral triangle.
- **Adductor brevis**: arises from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis and inserts on the upper linea aspera.
- **Adductor magnus**: the **adductor part** arises from the ischiopubic ramus, is supplied by the obturator nerve, and inserts on the linea aspera. The **hamstring part** arises from the ischial tuberosity, is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, and inserts on the **adductor tubercle**. The **adductor hiatus** between these parts lets the femoral vessels pass into the popliteal fossa.
- **Gracilis**: arises from the pubis and inserts on the medial proximal tibia in the **pes anserinus**. It is the only adductor that crosses the knee.
- **Obturator externus**: covers the outer surface of the obturator membrane. It acts as a lateral rotator.

**Obturator nerve (anterior divisions of L2-L4).** It descends along the medial border of psoas and passes through the obturator canal. There it divides into two branches that straddle adductor brevis:
- **Anterior division**: runs anterior to brevis. It supplies adductor longus, adductor brevis and gracilis, gives skin branches to the medial thigh, and sends a branch to the hip joint.
- **Posterior division**: runs posterior to brevis. It supplies obturator externus and the adductor part of magnus, and often sends a branch to the knee.

**Vessels.** The **obturator artery**, from the internal iliac artery, accompanies the nerve. The **profunda femoris** artery supplies most of the compartment through perforating branches.

**Function.** Beyond simple adduction, these muscles stabilize the pelvis during the stance phase of gait. They also assist hip flexion or extension, depending on the angle of the hip.
levels.phd:
**Developmental logic.** In the lumbar plexus, the obturator nerve forms from the **anterior (ventral) divisions** of L2-L4. The femoral nerve forms from the posterior (dorsal) divisions of the same roots. This explains why the adductors behave as "ventral" musculature.

Adductor magnus shows a **dual derivation**. Its ischiocondylar (hamstring) part is innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, consistent with its hamstring identity. Pectineus is variably innervated: usually by the femoral nerve, by the obturator nerve in a minority, and by both in some people. This reflects its position at the boundary between compartments.

An **accessory obturator nerve** (from L3-L4) is present in roughly 10-30% of dissections, depending on the series. It passes over the superior pubic ramus rather than through the canal, and it may supply pectineus and the hip joint.

**Hilton's law** holds here: the obturator nerve supplies the hip joint, the muscles that move it, and the overlying skin. Its articular branches to both the hip and the knee underlie **referred pain**. Hip pathology, classically a slipped capital femoral epiphysis in adolescents, may present as medial knee pain.

**Moment arms.** Adductor function depends on posture. With the hip flexed beyond roughly 60-70°, adductor longus shifts from a flexor moment toward an extensor moment. Adductor magnus has a large extensor moment arm and contributes substantially to hip extension, especially at deep flexion as in climbing or squatting.

Modelling and EMG studies show that the adductors fire in stance and swing. This suggests a role in controlling the limb in the frontal and sagittal planes rather than pure adduction. The cross-sectional area of the adductor group rivals that of the quadriceps.

**Vascular variation.** An **aberrant obturator artery** arising from the inferior epigastric artery occurs in about 20-30% of people. It crosses near the femoral ring (the classic "corona mortis" anastomosis region). This is relevant to the pelvic floor and hernia-adjacent anatomy and to the medial compartment's blood supply.

**Controversy.** It remains debated whether adductor-dominant groin pain arises mainly from the musculotendinous junction, the enthesis at the pubis, or the shared aponeurosis with rectus abdominis.
levels.expert:
**Groin pain in athletes.** The 2015 **Doha agreement** classifies groin pain into adductor-related, iliopsoas-related, inguinal-related and pubic-related entities, plus hip-related pain. Adductor-related pain is the most common. It is diagnosed by adductor tenderness and pain on resisted adduction, for example the squeeze test.

MRI often shows a **proximal adductor longus** injury, either an intratendinous tear or an enthesis avulsion. Complete proximal avulsions in elite athletes are increasingly repaired surgically, although conservative outcomes are often comparable. Prevention programs built on eccentric adduction work, such as the **Copenhagen adduction exercise**, reduce groin injury rates in soccer trials.

**Obturator nerve injury** is uncommon. Typical causes include:
- Pelvic surgery, such as lateral pelvic lymphadenectomy or retroperitoneal procedures
- Lithotomy positioning
- Pelvic fractures or acetabular fixation
- Obstetric compression
- Entrapment in athletes by a fascial band over the adductor brevis (obturator neuropathy)

Patients describe medial thigh pain or numbness and a weak, circumducting gait with difficulty crossing the legs. Because the cutaneous territory varies and may be small, sensory testing is unreliable. Weakness of adduction, plus EMG of the adductors, is more informative. Preserved quadriceps function distinguishes isolated obturator injury from a lumbar plexopathy or an L3-L4 radiculopathy.

**Procedural relevance.**
- During **transurethral resection of bladder tumours** on the lateral wall, electrical stimulation of the nearby obturator nerve can trigger a sudden **adductor jerk**, risking bladder perforation. An ultrasound-guided **obturator nerve block** is used to prevent this.
- Obturator branches to the hip are targets of **radiofrequency ablation** for chronic hip pain, often combined with femoral articular branch ablation (the PENG block concept).
- **Gracilis** is a workhorse free flap for facial reanimation. Its pedicle comes from the medial circumflex femoral or profunda femoris artery, and its motor branch is the anterior division of the obturator nerve.
- In **cerebral palsy**, adductor spasticity causes scissoring and hip subluxation. Management includes botulinum toxin injection, adductor tenotomy, or obturator neurectomy.

**Open questions.** How much of athletic groin pain is truly a nerve entrapment? And do hip-joint denervation strategies remain durable over time?

Most arise from the pubis/ischiopubic ramus and insert on the linea aspera
Obturator nerve: anterior divisions of L2-L4, exits via the obturator canal
Anterior and posterior divisions straddle adductor brevis
Adductor magnus hamstring part is supplied by the tibial nerve; pectineus usually by the femoral nerve
Hip disease can refer pain to the knee through the obturator nerve

lessons.title: Posterior Thigh: Hamstrings & the Sciatic Nerve

levels.kid:
Put your hand on the back of your thigh and bend your knee. Feel those muscles get hard? Those are your **hamstrings**. There are three of them, like three ropes that run from your bottom bone down past the back of your knee.

When they pull, they bend your knee and swing your leg back. That is how you push off when you run or climb stairs.

Right in the middle of them runs the **sciatic nerve**. It is the biggest nerve in your body, about as thick as your thumb! It is like a big phone cable carrying messages between your brain and your leg and foot.

Runners stretch their hamstrings because these muscles can get pulled when you sprint fast.
levels.hs:
The back (posterior) compartment of the thigh holds the **hamstrings**: three muscles that cross two joints, the hip and the knee.

- **Biceps femoris** (lateral side): has a long head and a short head, and inserts on the head of the fibula.
- **Semitendinosus** (medial): has a long, cord-like tendon at its lower end.
- **Semimembranosus** (medial, deeper): has a flat, membrane-like upper tendon.

All three true hamstrings start at the **ischial tuberosity**, the "sitting bone" of the pelvis. Because they cross both joints, they do two jobs: **extend the hip** (swing the thigh back) and **flex the knee** (bend it).

The **sciatic nerve** comes from the spinal nerve roots L4 to S3. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, usually below the piriformis muscle, and runs down the back of the thigh deep to the hamstrings, which it supplies. Usually just above the knee it splits into the **tibial nerve** and the **common fibular (peroneal) nerve**.

Real example: sprinters often get **hamstring strains**, especially in the biceps femoris long head. It happens late in the swing phase, when the muscle is stretched while working hard to slow the leg down before the foot hits the ground.
levels.college:
**Compartment and attachments.** The posterior thigh compartment is separated from the anterior and medial compartments by intermuscular septa. The true hamstrings share three features: origin from the ischial tuberosity, insertion on the tibia or fibula, and innervation by the **tibial division** of the sciatic nerve.
- **Semitendinosus**: inserts on the superomedial tibia as part of the **pes anserinus**, together with sartorius and gracilis.
- **Semimembranosus**: inserts on the posteromedial tibial condyle. It sends expansions that form the **oblique popliteal ligament** and reinforce the posteromedial knee capsule.
- **Biceps femoris long head**: arises from the ischial tuberosity. The **short head** arises from the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line. Both insert on the fibular head.

**Exceptions.** The short head of biceps crosses only the knee and is supplied by the **common fibular division**, so it is not a true hamstring. The **hamstring part of adductor magnus** comes from the ischial tuberosity and is supplied by the tibial division, so it behaves like a hamstring.

**Actions.** The hamstrings extend the hip and flex the knee. With the knee flexed, biceps femoris laterally rotates the leg, and the two semi- muscles medially rotate it. In gait they act as decelerators: they work eccentrically in late swing to slow knee extension.

**Sciatic nerve course.**
- Leaves via the greater sciatic foramen, inferior to piriformis.
- Passes between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity.
- Runs on adductor magnus and is crossed posteriorly by the long head of biceps.
- Splits at the apex of the popliteal fossa.

Its two divisions sit in a common sheath. The tibial division supplies all the hamstrings except the short head of biceps.

**Blood supply** comes mainly from the **perforating branches of the profunda femoris** artery. There is no major posterior axial artery in the thigh.

**Clinical.** Weakness of knee flexion together with foot drop and sensory loss below the knee, with sparing of the medial leg, points to a sciatic lesion. Sensation of the medial leg is spared because the saphenous nerve comes from the femoral nerve.
levels.phd:
**Architecture.** The hamstrings show distinct designs. Semimembranosus has short fibres and a large physiological cross-sectional area, suited to force. Semitendinosus has long fibres arranged in series and divided by a **tendinous inscription**, suited to excursion and speed. Biceps femoris long head is intermediate. It shares a proximal **conjoint tendon** with semitendinosus at the ischial tuberosity. Semimembranosus arises separately, lateral and anterior to that tendon.

**Injury biomechanics.** Sprint-type strains cluster at the proximal musculotendinous junction of the biceps femoris long head. Modelling studies (e.g., Thelen, Chumanov and colleagues) place peak musculotendon stretch and negative work in **late swing**, when the muscle decelerates the extending knee. Several factors are proposed to explain why biceps femoris long head is most affected:
- its greater stretch per unit of hip flexion;
- its dual innervation, since the long head is tibial-supplied while the adjacent short head is fibular-supplied, which may desynchronize activation;
- its fascicle architecture.

Dual innervation is a plausible but contested explanation.

**Nerve microanatomy.** The sciatic nerve is a composite nerve. Its tibial division comes from the anterior divisions of L4 to S3, and its common fibular division from the posterior divisions of L4 to S2. The two are bound by a shared epineurium but have separate fascicular groups. The fibular division lies laterally, has fewer and larger fascicles with less connective tissue, and is tethered at the fibular neck. This helps explain why fibular deficits dominate many proximal sciatic injuries.

**Piriformis variation.** Beaton and Anson's classic 1937 classification described how the nerve divisions relate to piriformis. A recent meta-analysis (Smoll 2010, about 6,000 limbs) found the usual pattern, the whole nerve passing below piriformis, in about 85–90%. The most common variant is the fibular division piercing piriformis. Whether these variants cause **piriformis syndrome** is still unproven.

**Vascular nuance.** The **companion artery of the sciatic nerve**, a branch of the inferior gluteal artery, is the remnant of the embryonic **axial (sciatic) artery**. When the axial artery persists, it is an anomaly that is prone to aneurysm.
levels.expert:
**Proximal avulsion.** Complete proximal hamstring tendon avulsions usually happen with forced hip flexion while the knee is extended, as in water-skiing or a slip into the splits. They are often missed early. MRI shows how many tendons are torn and how far they have retracted. Avulsion of all three tendons with retraction of more than about 2 cm is the usual threshold for considering surgery. Early repair, within about 4 to 6 weeks, avoids scarring around the sciatic nerve and fixed retraction. Approaches through a transverse gluteal-crease incision require identifying the **posterior femoral cutaneous nerve** and the sciatic nerve, which lies only about 1 to 2 cm lateral to the tuberosity. Neuropraxia from traction during repair is a recognized complication.

**Rehabilitation evidence.** The **Nordic hamstring exercise** builds eccentric strength and lengthens biceps femoris fascicles. Meta-analyses show that programmes including it substantially reduce hamstring injury rates, though adherence limits the benefit in practice. Injuries that involve the intramuscular or central tendon carry longer return-to-play times and more frequent re-injury. This has been formalized in the **British Athletic Muscle Injury Classification**.

**Sciatic injury pitfalls.**
- **Posterior hip dislocation and total hip arthroplasty (posterior approach).** These cause stretch or compression injury that affects mainly the fibular division. The result is foot drop that can mimic an L5 radiculopathy.
- **Distinguishing a peroneal-pattern sciatic lesion from an L5 root lesion or a fibular-neck lesion.** Test two muscles. The short head of biceps (the only thigh muscle supplied by the fibular division) on EMG localizes the lesion above the knee. Tibialis posterior (tibial nerve, L5) is weak in L5 radiculopathy but spared in fibular-neck palsy.
- **Intramuscular injection.** Gluteal injections that are misplaced medially and inferiorly endanger the nerve. This is why the upper-outer quadrant or the ventrogluteal site is used.

**Imaging and frontiers.** High-resolution MR neurography and ultrasound now show fascicular swelling, piriformis-related variants and post-traumatic neuromas. Deep gluteal syndrome is now framed as entrapment of the sciatic nerve anywhere in the subgluteal space, not only by piriformis. Endoscopic decompression is used for it, but the supporting evidence comes mostly from case series. Open questions remain: the reliability of diagnostic criteria, and whether distal nerve transfers improve the poor recovery of the fibular division after high sciatic injury, which is a key target in peripheral nerve surgery.

keyPoints: True hamstrings: semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris long head
They arise from the ischial tuberosity, extend the hip and flex the knee
Tibial division of the sciatic nerve supplies the hamstrings except the short head of biceps
Sciatic nerve (L4–S3) usually exits below piriformis and splits above the knee
Sprint strains hit biceps femoris long head in late swing (eccentric loading)
The fibular division is more vulnerable, so sciatic injuries often cause foot drop

test.q: Where do the true hamstrings take their origin?
test.explain: All three true hamstrings arise from the ischial tuberosity, the sitting bone.

test.q: What are the two main actions of the hamstrings?
test.explain: Crossing both joints posteriorly, they extend the hip and flex the knee.

test.q: Which posterior thigh muscle is supplied by the common fibular division?
test.explain: The short head of biceps is the one fibular-supplied thigh muscle; the others use the tibial division.

test.q: Where does biceps femoris insert?
test.explain: Both heads of biceps femoris insert on the fibular head, on the lateral side of the knee.

test.q: Which hamstring joins sartorius and gracilis at the pes anserinus?
test.explain: Semitendinosus inserts on the superomedial tibia as part of the pes anserinus.

test.q: The sciatic nerve usually leaves the pelvis by passing:
choices: Through the obturator foramen and canal
Through the lesser sciatic foramen alone
Deep to the inguinal ligament laterally
Below piriformis, via the greater foramen
test.explain: In about 85–90% of limbs the whole nerve exits below piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen.

test.q: Into which two nerves does the sciatic nerve usually divide?
test.explain: It splits near the apex of the popliteal fossa into the tibial and common fibular nerves.

test.q: During sprinting, hamstring strains most often happen in which phase?
test.explain: In late swing the hamstrings are stretched while contracting eccentrically to slow the leg down.

test.q: The main blood supply of the posterior thigh comes from:
test.explain: The perforating arteries of the deep femoral artery supply the posterior compartment.

test.q: Which hamstring has a long head and a short head?
test.explain: Biceps femoris has a long head from the ischial tuberosity and a short head from the linea aspera.

test.q: The sciatic nerve arises from spinal nerve roots L4 to ___.
test.explain: The sciatic nerve comes from L4–S3 of the sacral plexus.

test.q: Which hamstring has a flat, membrane-like upper tendon?
test.explain: Semimembranosus is named after its flat, membranous proximal tendon.

kidTest.q: Where are your hamstrings?
kidTest.explain: The hamstrings are on the back of your thigh.

kidTest.q: What do hamstrings help your knee do?
kidTest.explain: When they pull, they bend your knee.

kidTest.q: How many hamstring muscles are there?
kidTest.explain: There are three hamstrings.

kidTest.q: What is the sciatic nerve like?
kidTest.explain: It carries messages between your brain and your leg, like a cable.

kidTest.q: The biggest cable-like message carrier in your body, as thick as your thumb, is the sciatic n _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The sciatic nerve is the biggest nerve, about as thick as your thumb.

advancedTest.q: A patient has foot drop. EMG shows denervation in the short head of biceps femoris. The lesion is most likely:
choices: An L5 root lesion at the spine
A deep fibular nerve lesion in the leg
Sciatic nerve fibular division above the knee
Fibular nerve compression at the fibular neck
advancedTest.explain: The short head is the only thigh muscle supplied by the fibular division, so its involvement places the lesion above the knee. The fibular-neck lesion is tempting, but it lies below that branch.

advancedTest.q: Why are fibular deficits common after proximal sciatic injury?
choices: It has fewer, larger fascicles and is tethered distally
It runs medial to the tibial division in the sheath
It lacks a shared epineurium with the tibial division
Its fibres arise from anterior divisions of the plexus
advancedTest.explain: The fibular division has fewer, larger fascicles with less connective tissue and is tethered at the fibular neck, which makes it more vulnerable to stretch.

advancedTest.q: Why is adductor magnus's ischial part grouped functionally with the hamstrings?
choices: It inserts on the fibular head
It arises from the linea aspera
It is supplied by the obturator nerve
advancedTest.explain: It arises from the ischial tuberosity and is supplied by the tibial division, like the true hamstrings. Obturator supply belongs to the adductor part.

advancedTest.q: Why is early repair favoured for a complete avulsion of all three proximal hamstring tendons?
choices: Late repair has no proven effect on function
It avoids scarring around the sciatic nerve and fixed retraction
It allows the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve to be removed
The tendons heal reliably without surgery over time
advancedTest.explain: Delay leads to scarring around the sciatic nerve and fixed retraction, which make repair harder and risk nerve injury.
